description:
Purple tea is Kenya's own invention: a tea bush with purple leaves, developed over about 25 years by the Tea Research Foundation of Kenya and released to farmers around 2011 as clone TRFK 306. The colour comes from anthocyanins, the same pigments that make blueberries and red cabbage purple, and the tea made from it is marketed on those antioxidants as much as on taste.

The leaf is usually processed like a green tea, steamed or pan-fired and rolled, so that the pigments survive; some factories make lightly oxidised, oolong-like versions and a few make a fully oxidised black purple tea. It is grown mainly in the Nandi Hills and around Kericho and Kirinyaga, plucked year-round, with the dry-season leaf most intensely coloured.

The cup is pale pinkish-amber to reddish-violet and tastes light, smooth and mildly fruity with a woody note, a soft tartness and very little bitterness; it is more about colour and novelty than depth. A squeeze of lemon turns the liquor bright pink, because anthocyanins change colour with acidity. Brew it at around 85 °C for three minutes and re-steep twice.

It is sold by factory and year through direct importers and a handful of Kenyan brands, as loose leaf, tea bags and powder; there is no vintage, so buy within a year. Plenty of online sellers overstate the health claims; buy it for the novelty and the taste rather than as medicine.

If you like it, the same clone is sometimes made as a hand-rolled black tea, which has more body and keeps the pink trick.
history:
Purple tea comes out of Kenyan plant breeding rather than old tradition. The Tea Research Foundation of Kenya developed a purple-leaved assamica clone, TRFK 306, over about 25 years by its breeder's account. Its own paper describes the clone as pre-released for commercial use as an anthocyanin-rich tea, with yields comparable to the standard clone TRFK 31/8 and strong resistance to the main pests and diseases. A cultivar database and the trade press give 2011 as the release year.

It is not a separate type of tea: the leaf can be made into green or black tea like any other cultivar. Kenyan producers make it to order alongside their far larger black tea output, and much of the selling rests on health claims that go further than the evidence for this tea.
